segments.narration: Spy satellites caught a 92-metre machine the CIA said couldn't fly. Kaspiysk harbour, on the Caspian Sea, late 1960s. Low over the water, in plain sight.
Ten jet engines. Five hundred and forty-four tonnes loaded. A wingspan barely a third of the hull's length.
So how does half a thousand tonnes stay up on stubs like that? Analysts filed it as KASP-A and argued.
It rode a cushion of its own trapped air, metres above the surface. A ground-effect craft, designed by Rostislav Alexeyev. Soviet engineers called it an ekranoplan.
First flight, October 1966. For twenty-two years nothing bigger flew anywhere, until pilot error dropped it into the Caspian in 1980.

research.summary: The KM (Korabl Maket), nicknamed the Caspian Sea Monster, was a Soviet ground-effect vehicle built by the Central Hydrofoil Design Bureau to Rostislav Alexeyev's design. It was 92 m long with a 37.6 m wingspan, had ten Dobrynin RD-7 turbojets, a maximum takeoff weight of 544 tonnes, and flew just metres above the water, which is how such short wings carried it. US intelligence photographed it at Kaspiysk by reconnaissance satellite in the late 1960s and catalogued it as KASP-A. It first flew on 16 October 1966, was the largest aircraft in the world until the An-225 flew in 1988, and was destroyed in 1980 when pilot error put it into the sea; it floated for about a week, sank, and was never recovered.

factual_claims.text: Two skeletons excavated at Cladh Hallan on South Uist in 2001 were each assembled from the bones of at least three different individuals.

Ancient mitochondrial DNA published in 2012 showed the mandible, right humerus and right femur of one Cladh Hallan skeleton came from different individuals, and its female-type pelvis was paired with a male-type skull and jaw.
The bodies were kept for centuries before burial: one man died about 1600 BC and the woman about 1300 BC, and neither was buried until roughly 1120 BC.
Limited demineralisation of the outer bone, with radiocarbon dating, indicates the bodies spent roughly 6 to 18 months in a peat bog shortly after death, which halted decay.
Researchers including Mike Parker Pearson have suggested the composites merged separate ancestral identities or lines of descent into one body, and the purpose remains uncertain.

segments.narration: This skeleton was built from three different people. South Uist, in the Outer Hebrides. Dug out from under a Bronze Age house floor in 2001.
The pelvis read female. The skull and jaw read male. DNA work in 2012 showed the jaw, the arm and the leg came from three bodies.
Who assembles a person out of spare parts? Someone who had been keeping those parts for centuries. One of these men died around 1600 BC.
The bone chemistry points to months in a peat bog. The acid stopped the decay. Then the bodies were lifted back out again.
He was not buried until about 1120 BC. The leading reading is deliberate: separate ancestors merged into one body, for reasons still argued over.

research.summary: Cladh Hallan, on South Uist in the Outer Hebrides, is the only site in Great Britain where prehistoric mummies have been found. Excavations running 1988-2002 recovered remains beneath the floors of roundhouses built c. 1080-1020 BCE; what looked like four individuals in 2001 proved to be composite bodies. Ancient mitochondrial DNA reported by Hanna and colleagues in the Journal of Archaeological Science in 2012 showed that the mandible, right humerus and right femur of one skeleton came from different individuals, and osteology found a female-consistent pelvis with a male-type skull and jaw. Radiocarbon dates put one man's death near 1600 BCE and the woman's near 1300 BCE, with burial only around 1120 BCE, so the remains were curated for roughly 500 and 180 years. Limited demineralisation of the bone surfaces, read with the radiocarbon dates, indicates about 6 to 18 months in a peat bog shortly after death. Why the bodies were assembled is unsettled; Mike Parker Pearson has suggested the mixing merged ancestral identities or lines of descent.

research.summary: Çatalhöyük is a Neolithic settlement on the Konya Plain in southern Anatolia, Turkey, occupied from about 7100 BC to about 5600 BC. Its dwellings were packed together in a honeycomb-like maze with no footpaths or streets between them; most were entered through holes in the ceiling reached by ladders, and those openings were also the only ventilation for hearth and oven smoke, so the rooftops functioned as the streets. The dead were buried in pits beneath the floors, especially under hearths, platforms and beds, with early burials featuring closely related families and later ones including more unrelated individuals. As many as eighteen levels of settlement have been uncovered. James Mellaart found the site in 1958 and dug four seasons from 1961; Ian Hodder's project ran 1993-2018. A 2025 genetic study suggests early matrilocality and matrilineality, with households passing from mother to daughter.

research.summary: Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire from the 7th to the 14th centuries. Theophanes the Confessor credits its development around 672 to Kallinikos (Callinicus of Heliopolis), an architect who fled to the Romans, and it was first used against Arab fleets during the siege of Constantinople of 674-678. It was projected under pressure through a bronze tube called a siphon, usually mounted near a ship's prow, with a portable cheirosiphon for land use, and it burned on water. The recipe was a compartmentalised state secret - no single operator knew the whole system - and was eventually lost; Bulgarians who captured 36 siphons and some of the substance in 814 could not use them. Most modern scholars hold it was petroleum-based (crude or refined naphtha) mixed with resins, comparable to napalm, with earlier saltpetre and quicklime theories rejected. John Haldon and Maurice Byrne proposed a reconstruction in 1977, and Haldon's 2002 full-scale test using crude oil and wood resins reached a flame temperature above 1,000 degrees Celsius with a range of up to 15 metres, the stream curving downward rather than arcing up.

factual_claims.text: Monte Testaccio in Rome is an artificial mound of broken pottery about 35 metres high and nearly 1 kilometre in circumference, containing an estimated 53 million amphorae.

The amphorae were mostly Dressel 20 vessels from Baetica in southern Spain carrying olive oil, around 6 billion litres in total, with up to 130,000 amphorae deposited a year at the late-2nd-century AD peak.
Broken Roman pottery was normally reused, including as aggregate in concrete and as landfill.
Dressel 20 fragments were large and curved and hard to crush small enough for reuse, and residual oil reacting with lime would have weakened concrete, so discarding them was cheaper.

The mound was engineered in stepped terraces with retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae, lime was sprinkled over the shards probably to mask the smell of rancid oil, and painted tituli picti on the vessels record the oil's weight, the weighers' names and the district of origin.

segments.narration: A Roman hill is made of 53 million broken jars. Thirty-five metres high, nearly a kilometre around. All of it thrown away.
Every jar carried olive oil from southern Spain to feed the city. Around six billion litres. At the peak, 130,000 jars a year.
Rome recycled almost everything. Broken pottery normally went back into concrete. So why smash these and carry the pieces uphill?
Oil-soaked clay wrecks concrete, and these jars broke into curved slabs too big to crush. Dumping them was simply cheaper.
So Rome engineered its dump. Stepped terraces, retaining walls of whole jars, lime for the stink. Painted labels on the pots still record every weight and inspector.

research.summary: Monte Testaccio is an artificial mound in Rome made almost entirely of broken Roman amphorae: about 35 metres high, nearly 1 kilometre in circumference, covering some 2 hectares, with a volume of roughly 580,000 cubic metres and an estimated 53 million vessels. Excavated deposits date to about AD 140-250, with dumping possibly beginning in the 1st century BC and ending around the 260s. Most of the pots are Dressel 20 amphorae from Baetica in the Guadalquivir valley of modern Spain, with smaller numbers from Tripolitania and Byzacena; all carried olive oil, roughly 6 billion litres in total, with up to 130,000 amphorae a year deposited at the late-2nd-century peak and most vessels holding about 70 litres. Broken pottery was normally reused in concrete or as landfill, but Dressel 20 sherds were large and curved and hard to crush, and residual oil reacts with lime to weaken concrete, so disposal was cheaper. The mound was carefully engineered: stepped terraces, retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae filled with sherds, and lime sprinkled over the shards, probably to mask the smell of rancid oil. Painted inscriptions (tituli picti) record the oil's weight, the names of those who weighed and documented it, and the district where it was bottled, showing state-authorised imports for the annona.

research.summary: The Vinland Map is a 20th-century forgery presented as a 15th-century mappa mundi showing Vinlanda Insula southwest of Greenland. It surfaced in 1957 bound with the genuine Tartar Relation, was sold for $3,500 to dealer Laurence C. Witten II, and was bought for about $300,000 by Yale alumnus Paul Mellon, who donated it on condition of secrecy until a scholarly book appeared; it was revealed the day before Columbus Day, 1965. Walter McCrone's team found anatase titanium dioxide in the ink in 1972, a pigment form made commercially only from the 1920s; Raman work by Brown and Clark confirmed it in 2002, and Yale's Richard Hark reported the same in 2018. Yale's 2021 X-ray fluorescence and Raman survey found titanium and barium throughout the ink lines with little to no iron, sulfur or copper, unlike genuine 15th-century manuscripts in the same collection, and infrared imaging showed the bound Tartar Relation had text altered in modern ink. research.summary: The Maya Codex of Mexico, long known as the Grolier Codex and renamed Codice Maya de Mexico by Mexico's INAH in 2018, is a pre-Columbian Maya screenfold almanac tracking Venus. Of an original 20 pages, 10 survive. It appeared in a private collection in the 1960s; Mexican collector Dr Josue Saenz said he was flown in 1965 to an airstrip near Tortuguero, Tabasco, and shown it, and it was first exhibited at the Grolier Club in New York from 20 April to 5 June 1971. Its authenticity was doubted from the start, partly for its looted, context-free origin, with J. Eric S. Thompson questioning it in 1975 without examining it. Radiocarbon tests gave 1035-1431 CE (1972), 1050-1284 CE (2012) and 1021-1154 CE (2018). Coe, Miller, Houston and Taube argued for authenticity in 2015, and in 2018 INAH-coordinated teams declared it authentic, citing gypsum-base paper preparation, pigments contemporaneous with the paper (lamp black, hematite red, Maya blue with palygorskite, cochineal browns) and at least three periods of high moisture, and confirming it as the oldest surviving book of the Americas.

research.summary: Bog butter is an ancient waxy substance recovered from peat bogs, chiefly in Ireland and Scotland, found inside wooden buckets, kegs, barrels, dishes and churns, often well sealed and sometimes lined with a deerskin bladder or plant fibres. In Ireland the practice dates back to the first century AD. On 28 April 2011 press reports described about 50 kg (110 lb) of bog butter found in Ballard Bog near Tullamore, County Offaly, by Brian and Joe Clancy while cutting turf: a carved wooden vessel about 30 cm in diameter and 60 cm tall, buried about 2.3 m down, still carrying a faint dairy smell. Until 2003 the origin of bog butter was uncertain; University of Bristol researchers then found some samples were adipose or tallow and others dairy. Leading explanations for burial are preservation (bogs are cold, low in oxygen and acidic, and Daniel C. Fisher's experiments found meat buried up to two years had bacterial counts comparable to freezer-stored controls), primitive food processing, and hiding a luxury from raiders in early medieval Ireland. Press age estimates for the Tullamore vessel ranged from 2,000 to 5,000 years and no peer-reviewed radiocarbon result for that vessel was located, so no age for it is asserted in the script.

segments.narration: Four kilometres under Antarctic ice, a lake never froze. Vostok runs 250 kilometres long, fifty wide, and up to 900 metres deep.
Its water sits near minus three degrees and stays liquid anyway, squeezed by hundreds of bars of pressure from the ice overhead.
It has been sealed off from the sky for roughly fifteen million years. So what has been living down there all that time?

research.summary: Lake Vostok is a subglacial lake in central East Antarctica, beneath Russia's Vostok Station, about 4,000 m below the ice surface. It is 250 km long, up to 50 km wide, covers 12,500 square kilometres, averages 432 m deep with a maximum depth reported between 510 and 900 m, and holds about 5,400 cubic kilometres of water. Its average temperature is about -3 degrees Celsius and it remains liquid under pressure reported at 345 to 355 bars. The water is estimated to have been sealed from the atmosphere about 15 million years ago (the lead gives 15 to 25 million years; news coverage gives 15 to 20). Andrey Kapitsa proposed the lake from 1959 and 1964 Soviet seismic soundings, British airborne radar in 1973 detected liquid water, J. P. Ridley confirmed it from ERS-1 satellite data in 1993, and the discovery was published in Nature on 20 June 1996. Russian drilling reached the lake's upper water surface in February 2012 (5 February for the completed 3,768 m core, 6 February for reaching water; Talalay gives contact at 3,769.3 m), through a borehole kept open with about 60 short tons of Freon and kerosene. Contamination has dogged the biology: researchers including David Pearce and Sergey Bulat questioned whether reported DNA came from the lake or the drill fluid, and in May 2017 Russian researchers reported their water samples were too contaminated to yield reliable chemical or biological data.
